text: Splash-m1 reports requests, time to first token, inter-token latency, prefill/decode rates, draft acceptance, prefix-cache hits, context, memory and thermal state via /status; the production ds3 build adds per-verify-cycle speculative decoding (from ds2) and GPU-side router aggregates (routes per layer and expert, counted by the MoE grouping kernel and read without a GPU command or wait), optional sampled selections (row 0 of one decode step in 8) and PLE row-store aggregates, within run-to-run noise of ds2. About 90 % of the useful native-era visualisation is restored. Still unavailable: router gate weights, the expert selections of every speculative row (they are counted in the aggregates, not sampled), per-token PLE reads (reported per interval), and per-request prompt rows where the runtime records none. These reduce granularity, not the operational views; nothing is estimated.

Speculative decoding uses the shared DFlash2 draft trained for the base Qwen3.8-Flash-Next; it is verified by each model, so outputs are unaffected. Because DFlash2 is feature-conditioned on the target's hidden states at a fixed set of layers, it tracks Swift and Cyber (same architecture and tokenizer) well: measured acceptance on one coding prompt was Scope 73%, Cyber 70%, Swift MEDIUM 61%. A per-model draft could lift this but is not worth building at current acceptance; see docs/DRAFT-MODELS.md.

Data-free 2-bit expert encoding flattens Cyber's opening distribution: 4 of 80 sampled openings of one agent request stopped after a few junk tokens (Scope and Swift 0 of 80); 2 of 21 historical agent sessions needed a retry. A calibrated re-encode is deferred.
The source is a W4A4 export; no Apple runtime reproduces its 4-bit activations, so the build is weight-faithful with full-precision activations.
Cyber has no refusal behaviour; in Full Auto, text in a page, file or screenshot can steer its tools without an approval step.

Cyber runs closest to the Metal limit: its 128K plan is 50.81 GiB against a 51.84 GiB recommended working set (1.03 GiB headroom), which is why it prefills in 1024-token chunks. A 1536-token chunk (plan 51.37 GiB) was started but not validated at depth and is not used.
Tokenizer conformance 257 of 339 on the unpatched runtime: no NFC normalization and 24 rarely-typed special tokens tokenized as text.
Video input is not exposed; the agent stack has no video path.
Zed's ACP thinking option cannot select reasoning effort, so each profile is its own editor entry.
dwarfstar-acp and Workstation chats never load a model; start it from the Workstation (or dwarfstar switch) first.
The KimiCU Calculator check was not re-run for Cyber XHIGH and Swift MEDIUM (screen locked at the time); it passed on Cyber LOW.

The reported Cyber MEDIUM -> Stop -> LOW failure was not reproduced exactly from the user's run (the service log of that run was not kept). The real-runtime gate found and fixed three lifecycle races that produce that class of failure while the window is open (ledger removal racing a status poll, stale cached state after a stop, telemetry session not finalized); the reported sequence and the full matrix now pass through the installed app's service and through the UI.

The Visualizer's request history is built from the per-cycle channel (ds2 and later), which reports decode cycles, not request ids. A request there is one uninterrupted decode run, split after 400 ms with no cycle; agent turns always separate (tool time and prefill produce no cycles), but two clients decoding at once would share one entry. History lives in the window only (last 20 requests, first 4,096 cycles each) and is gone on reload. On ds3 a request's routing is assigned by engine time to the decode run it overlaps: exact inside the run, approximate at its first and last ~180 ms interval.

Persistent records are versioned from 1.0.0 (chat schema 2). Builds before 1.0.0 accept only chat schema 1: before running one on migrated data, stop the service and run `bin/dwarfstar migrate --rollback --apply` (lossless; this release migrates forward again at start). A Workstation service started before a migration keeps the old code until it is restarted.

Workspace Auto and Full Auto depend on four exact edits to the Oh My Pi agent 18.4.5 bundle (acp/omp-patch.json, applied by `bin/dwarfstar agent-patch --apply`). Another agent version is refused, not guessed: updating the agent needs a new patch record. The launcher refuses an agent whose bundle no longer matches the permission record.

Workspace Auto confines writes to the chat's workspace and denies the Workstation service's port, but allows outbound network (the browser and web tools need it) and reads of the tool locations it lists. Full Auto has no sandbox at all. Neither is a defence against a hostile model: the presets limit accidents, not intent.

The setup guide and `doctor` only check and explain. Nothing is installed or downloaded for you: model files (about 70 GB per model), the runtime build, Bun, the agent and its browser are explicit steps in docs/REPRODUCIBILITY.md.

Chat folders nest two levels deep (Projects / DwarfStar), and a folder cannot be moved under another one; rename it, or create the new one and move its chats. Folders are Workstation metadata, so Zed's agent panel lists conversations without them.
